The protracted embryonic development, lasting about three years [ab = about three years] at the cold temperatures typical of their deep-sea habitat (6.9 °C [T = 6.9 °C]), yields pups that are relatively large and well-developed at parturition. Newborn individuals weigh roughly 268 grams [Wwb = roughly 268 grams] upon emergence, a value that aligns with the considerable egg diameter of around 8 centimeters observed in this species. This substantial birth mass is thought to enhance early survival by allowing neonates to better withstand periods of prey scarcity encountered in the mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones they inhabit. The extended gestation, among the longest documented for any elasmobranch, is a direct consequence of the low metabolic rates imposed by the perpetually cold, oxygen-poor waters below the thermocline. Consequently, females likely produce pups at infrequent intervals, investing considerable energy into each offspring rather than producing numerous small young.

As juveniles progress through their early years, growth proceeds at a slow but steady pace within their deepwater environment. This marked sexual dimorphism in size at maturation is a common pattern among deep-sea sharks, often linked to the energetic demands of gestation on females. Following the onset of puberty, males continue to grow, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of about 133 centimeters [Li = about 133 centimeters]. The corresponding maximal wet weight for adult males is roughly 21,800 grams [Wwi = roughly 21,800 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The time from birth to sexual maturity is estimated at approximately 5 years after parturition [tp = approximately 5 years after parturition], a delay that reflects the necessity for considerable body growth prior to the commencement of reproductive activity in an environment with unpredictable food resources.

Females ultimately achieve a larger maximum body size than males, attaining an ultimate total length of approximately 150 centimeters [Li = approximately 150 centimeters] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of about 31,700 grams [Wwi = about 31,700 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size likely reflects the substantial physical capacity required to support the lengthy gestation and the large litter sizes characteristic of the species. The reproductive output of a fully mature female is considerable; litters typically contain up to 23 pups [N_R_i = up to 23 pups] per reproductive event. However, the frequency of such events is remarkably low, with available data suggesting that individual females may only produce a single litter every five years [F_R_i = a single litter every five years]. The overall pace of life for Centroscymnus plunketi is remarkably protracted, a direct consequence of the cold, stable thermal regime of its deep-sea habitat. This extreme longevity, combined with an age at birth of roughly 1,095 days [ab = roughly 1,095 days] under the ambient thermal conditions of 6.9 °C [T = 6.9 °C], means that individual sharks do not recruit into the adult population until they are already several years old. Following parturition, the slow growth rate means that many years elapse before the onset of gonadal maturation. The combination of a very late age at maturity, exceptionally low fecundity, and an extraordinarily long generation time results in a demographic profile that is among the most K-selected of any vertebrate, bearing closer resemblance to that of some large whales or elephants than to most other fishes.

The life-history strategy of the Plunket shark is exquisitely tuned to the low-energy, stable environment of the continental slopes and abyssal plains it occupies from depths of several hundred to over a thousand meters. The deep-sea habitat imposes extreme constraints on metabolic rate and activity levels, and this species has evolved a suite of adaptations including an enlarged liver for buoyancy and energy storage that can constitute a substantial fraction of total body mass. Feeding ecology is characterized by opportunistic predation on teleosts, cephalopods, and other elasmobranchs, with stomach content analyses revealing a diet that reflects the low productivity of the bathyal zone. Population structure remains poorly understood, but the extreme life-history parameters documented here suggest that even modest increases in adult mortality from bycatch in deepwater fisheries can take decades to be offset by recruitment. Conservation efforts must therefore prioritize the protection of adult and sub-adult individuals to ensure population persistence.
